What the original study did not say

Grit: more than talent?

It was presented as the key to success. A 2017 review found it closely resembles a well-known trait: conscientiousness.

In 2007, the psychologist Angela Duckworth defined grit as the combination of passion and perseverance for long-term goals. Her studies showed it predicted who completed the gruelling first summer at the West Point military academy or who went far in a spelling bee. Her TED talk and 2016 book were a worldwide success.

What the meta-analysis found

In 2017, Marcus Credé and colleagues reviewed 88 studies. Grit did predict performance, but modestly, and it overlapped almost entirely with conscientiousness, one of the Big Five personality traits studied for decades. Moreover, the perseverance component predicted better than the passion component.

Duckworth herself has warned against using it to assess pupils or schools. Perseverance helps, but success also depends on opportunities, support and, sometimes, knowing when to give up on a goal.

References

  1. Duckworth, A. L. et al. (2007). Grit: perseverance and passion for long-term goals. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 92(6), 1087–1101.
  2. Credé, M., Tynan, M. C. y Harms, P. D. (2017). Much ado about grit. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 113(3), 492–511.
